newsitem.title: CANADA: FEATURE-Canada's Ben Heppner -- the Fourth Tenor?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Canada's Ben Heppner -- the Fourth Tenor?.

text.p: With opera's Three Tenors ageing, the music world wonders who can fill their enormous shoes.
Canada's most famous opera star, Ben Heppner, 40, modestly insists he does not aspire to join their elite group. But he cannot avoid the inevitable comparisons that are being made.

He and Roberto Alagna, a dashing Franco-Sicilian in his early 30s, are the two tenors most often mentioned as successors to the towering trio, even if they do not yet have the same stature or draw the same million dollars a night.

"Luciano Pavarotti, Jose Carreras and even Placido Domingo have arguably passed their vocal prime. Ben Heppner has arguably yet to reach his," Toronto Star music critic William Littler wrote recently.
"Mr. Heppner simply has no peers among helden tenors at the moment," The New York Times' James Oestreich wrote about a year ago, using a term for tenors who are able to sing Wagnerian roles.
Alagna emerged on the opera scene later than Heppner but is being marketed more aggressively as The Fourth Tenor.

Heppner protested before a performance in Ottawa that he was not gunning for Pavarotti. "It is not something to which I aspire. At this point I don't employ a publicity agent. It's amazing to me that I've gotten any notice at all," he told Reuters. "There's a huge price to pay for having your name a household name and I'm not willing to pay that at this point."

Heppner has an imposing presence on stage -- he looks bigger even than Pavarotti, although he will not divulge his weight -- and a powerful voice described by the journal Opera Canada as "liquid gold that is even from top to bottom."

He describes himself as a big-voiced lyric, able to power arias to a high C or melt into a pianissimo. He has already performed in the world's foremost opera houses from New York's Metropolitan to London's Covent Garden and Milan's La Scala.
DELIBERATE PACE

But he reckons he has time to achieve superstardom, and he has won praise for his deliberate pace in developing his voice and his repertoire. He does only 50 performances a year rather than the 75 to 100 some other stars undertake.

His says this is partly to protect his voice, partly to make sure he excels at everything he attempts and partly to have something to look forward to. He is only now working up the male title role in Wagner's demanding Tristan und Isolde, which he will perform in Seattle in the summer of 1998.

"It takes a certain experience level to deserve to give it a try," Heppner said, dressed in jeans and sipping tea in his hotel room. "It's such a crucial piece in my repertoire and in the development of opera. ... In a historical sense it's quite a pinnacle."

Verdi's Otello "is still a ways away," added Heppner, who has bookings with major opera houses into the next millenium. "I don't want to do all the big stuff in the next two or three years. Where to you go in the next 15 years?"
Another reason for his deliberate pace is his wish to protect and spend time with his wife of 17 years and his daughter and two sons, who live with him in a Toronto suburb.

"My daughter Ashleigh came home from school one day after there was this big publicity campaign in Toronto to get people to see Pagliacci (in which he played the title clown) ... She came home and said, 'Dad, I'm sick and tired of talking about your career.' She preferred to be liked because of who she was," he said. "I'd rather be known as Ashleigh's father rather than the other way around."

Whenever he can he gets to his sons Aaron and Lowell's hockey games and said he was even "hornswoggled" into coaching Aaron's little league baseball team one seaon. "My son got to suffer in some of the worst baseball coaching ever known to man, but we were together," he said.

Although his worldwide performances take him from home far more than he would like, he tries to take one child along for a few days in Munich or Boston or Toulouse or London from time to time to "spoil them rotten."
FROM HYMNS TO ELVIS
Heppner grew up in a big, singing British Columbia family himself, where hymns around the piano alternated with pieces like Elvis Presley's "You Ain't Nothing but a Hound Dog."
Deeply religious, he continues to boom out the occasional solo at his local Christian Missionary Alliance church or at a Billy Graham crusade.

He suffered through the second half of 1996 with the effects of a throat infection he contracted in Buenos Aires, forcing him to cancel some of his performances. But he is set to proceed to Chicago from January to March for Puccini's Turandot, to Vienna for Wagner's The Flying Dutchman and Lohengrin in April and on to Minneapolis and Geneva in May.

Of course, to paraphrase Mark Twain, rumours of the passing of the Three Tenors are greatly exaggerated. It is likely to be years before either Heppner or Alagna has a chance to wear one of their crowns.
